references.text: The command to love your neighbor as yourself is given in Leviticus 18:5, and the expert in the law asks Jesus who his neighbor is in order to justify himself in light of this command.
The core command "you shall love your neighbor as yourself" comes from this verse. The expert in the law's question "who is my neighbor?" is an attempt to limit the scope of this command.

The preceding conversation where the expert in the law asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and Jesus points to the law—including the command to love your neighbor. The question in verse 29 follows directly from this dialogue.
Jesus tells the Pharisees that they justify themselves before people, but God knows their hearts. The expert in the law's desire to "justify himself" (δικαιῶσαι ἑαυτόν) reflects the same attitude.
The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector is about self-justification versus true humility before God, which is the same theme as when the expert in the law wants to justify himself.
Paul describes those who seek to establish their own righteousness and do not submit to God's righteousness—parallel to the expert in the law's attempt to justify himself.
Paul states that no one is justified by the law, which sheds light on the expert in the law's attempt to justify himself through a narrow interpretation of the commandment to love your neighbor.

James quotes the command to love your neighbor as yourself and warns against showing favoritism. The expert in the law's question about who his neighbor is touches precisely on this: who deserves love.
